- When sentiment is consistently negative (e.g., < 0.33) and supply net is large negative, model tends to overcorrect upward — reduce forecast slope or cap upward momentum.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >+5% from prior 30d mean), model often overshoots and fails to adjust — apply downward drag or lagged mean reversion to prevent overextension.
- In high-event periods (e.g., >15 events/30d), model underestimates downside risk — increase downward bias or add volatility penalty to forecast.
- When bullish sentiment is low but supply net is negative, model often ignores bearish pressure — adjust forecast downward by 1–2% of recent 30d mean.
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles, model may misread trend — use sentiment-weighted moving average to smooth out short-term noise.
- In low-event periods (e.g., <10 events/30d), model tends to overestimate stability — add small downward drift or volatility buffer to prevent false confidence.
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, model often fails to anticipate sharp drops — apply “bearish lag” rule: if last 3 days sentiment < 0.33, reduce forecast by 0.5–1.5% per day.
- Model often ignores sentiment reversal — if sentiment shifts from positive to negative within 3 days, adjust forecast downward by 1–2% of current value.
- In high-bearish sentiment + high supply net, model tends to overestimate recovery — apply “mean reversion” rule: forecast = prior 30d mean + 0.5×(current - prior 30d mean) if sentiment < 0.33.
